design_detail: Matters Arising (Nature Medicine 27:1687–1688; received 3 June 2021, accepted 1 September 2021, published online 11 October 2021) by two psychiatrists and neuromodulation researchers at the University of Toronto, the second of two Matters Arising on MAPP1 (Mitchell et al., 2021). Eight running-text paragraphs and 10 references, without methods or data of its own; an unnumbered third page carries the acknowledgements, author contributions and competing interests. It argues that an inert placebo cannot blind a trial of a psychedelic drug, that MAPP1's own figures show that most participants may have known their group, and that the resulting unequal distribution of placebo (and nocebo) effects makes the trial hard to interpret within the usual placebo-controlled framework. Locators count paragraphs that start on each printed page (p. 1687: six; p. 1688: two, the second ending at the top of the right column).
can_establish: What the authors argue about blinding and placebo effects in MAPP1 and in psychedelic trials generally, and the upper bound on correct guesses that they derive from the trial's own figures.
cannot_establish: How much of MAPP1's difference between arms is due to expectancy, placebo or nocebo effects rather than to MDMA: the letter adds no data, and its 90% figure is an upper bound derived from counts that the trial's authors call anecdotal and give as minimums.

sample.recruitment: Not applicable (commentary). The trial discussed is MAPP1: 90 dosed adults with severe PTSD (Mitchell et al., 2021).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Not applicable; the authors chose their sources: the trial, two reviews of placebo and nocebo effects, one review of differential placebo effects in brain stimulation (by the first author), a ketamine trial with a midazolam control, the 2019 pooled phase 2 MDMA analysis, a psilocybin-versus-escitalopram trial, the CONSORT 2010 paper on testing blinding, a BMJ article arguing for blinding tests and a study of placebo psychedelic experiences (References 1-10, p. 1688).
sample.selection_effects: The placebo and nocebo arguments rest on general reviews and on studies in other conditions and treatments; no data from MAPP1's participants on expectations, guesses during treatment or nocebo responses are cited, because none were collected.

exposure.measurement: Not applicable. The letter describes MAPP1's comparison as MDMA versus an inert pill, both groups also receiving psychotherapy (p. 1687, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs).

comparison.controls: The letter discusses the inactive placebo used in MAPP1 and two alternatives: an active placebo that mimics the acute effects (midazolam in ketamine trials; a low or very low dose of the same drug, as with low-dose MDMA in some phase 2 MDMA trials) and an active comparator (escitalopram in a psilocybin trial) (p. 1687, 6th paragraph, continued on p. 1688).

outcomes.instruments: None of its own. The letter discusses blinding integrity (participants' guesses of their allocation) and placebo and nocebo effects as influences on reported outcomes.
outcomes.operationalization: Not applicable; 'correct guess' is derived from MAPP1's report of participants who wrongly believed they were in the other group when told their allocation.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not discussed: the letter does not mention MAPP1's blinded independent raters, and discusses only the blinding of participants.

analysis.effect_sizes: None computed by the authors beyond the share of possible correct guesses: 81 of 90 (90%), described as the number who may have correctly guessed their treatment at the end of the intervention (p. 1687, 3rd paragraph). Editors' check: MAPP1 reports that at least 7 of 44 on placebo and at least 2 of 46 on MDMA believed they were in the other group (at least 9 of 90), so 81 of 90 is the most who could have guessed correctly, not an observed count.
analysis.selective_reporting: The letter cites MAPP1's admission that blinding was challenging but not its blinded independent raters, the substantial improvement in its placebo arm (which bears on the nocebo argument), its adverse-event recording or its exclusion of positive drug effects from adverse-event collection. It names low-dose MDMA in phase 2 trials as an active-placebo option, citing the 2019 pooled phase 2 analysis (reference 6), which was retracted in August 2024 (after the letter).

interpretation_gap.results_show: A methodological argument: with an inert placebo and a drug with immediate, recognisable effects, participants are likely to know their allocation, so the MDMA arm receives the drug's effect plus the placebo effect of knowing it got the drug, and the placebo arm may lose placebo effects and gain nocebo effects; the trial's own figures allow up to 90% correct guesses; active placebos or comparators may help but have their own limits; investigators should at least measure blinding; and the alternative, judging treatments by absolute rather than placebo-relative benefit, would require changing how efficacy is measured. The letter concedes that the MDMA group improved markedly and asks how, not whether, it improved.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The letter says that the inert pill was, as expected, insufficient for successful blinding (p. 1687, 3rd paragraph), and that participants on MDMA had "an unfair boon of placebo effects" while those on placebo may have had nocebo effects (5th paragraph); both are inferences from design and from general placebo research, with no data from the trial on expectations or on guesses during treatment. Its 90% is presented with the hedge 'may have', which is accurate for an upper bound. It does not consider that MAPP1's placebo arm improved substantially with the same therapy, which a strong nocebo effect would make less likely, and it does not estimate how large the bias could be.

timeline.event: MAPP1, the trial discussed: blinding not formally assessed; at least 9 of 90 participants wrongly believed they were in the other group when told their allocation.
Halvorsen, Naudet & Cristea, the other Matters Arising on MAPP1, on benchmarking against first-line psychotherapies (it does not discuss blinding).
Mitchell, Coker & Yazar-Klosinski reply to both letters: blinding in psychedelic trials is a tremendous challenge with no perfect solution, and no flawless comparator exists.
MAPP2 includes an end-of-study blinding survey (94% on MDMA and 75% on placebo identified their group), the kind of measurement the letter asks for.
The sponsor's briefing document for the FDA advisory committee describes its bias-minimisation measures but reports neither the blinding survey nor any measure of expectancy.
Brett & Bynum's systematic review counts functional unblinding in four of six MAPS-linked trials.

replication.where_it_stands: The letter's central point, that an inactive placebo could not keep participants blind, was borne out in MAPP2's end-of-study survey; how much bias this introduced in either trial remains unestimated, because neither trial measured expectancy or asked about allocation during treatment, and no trial with an active placebo has been reported in the sources read.

funding.declared_conflicts: The authors declare no competing interests (Competing interests, third page of the PDF). The acknowledgements state that the content is the authors' opinion and not the official view of the University of Toronto or Harvard Medical School and their affiliated academic health care centres.
funding.affiliations_note: Department of Psychiatry and Division of Neurology, Temerty Faculty of Medicine, University of Toronto; Harquail Centre for Neuromodulation and Hurvitz Brain Sciences Program, Sunnybrook Research Institute; Division of Cognitive Neurology, Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center, Harvard Medical School (Burke); Temerty Centre for Therapeutic Brain Intervention, Centre for Addiction and Mental Health, Toronto (Blumberger) (p. 1687, footnote). M.J.B. conceived and drafted the letter, D.M.B. conceived it and revised it (third page). One of the 10 references is by the first author (reference 4).

what_would_settle_it: A trial of MDMA-assisted therapy that measures participants' expectations before treatment and their guesses of allocation after each session (and the raters' guesses), with an active placebo that produces noticeable effects, so that the difference between arms can be analysed against what participants believed they received.

domains.note: A letter; sources chosen by the authors, no search.

The trial's figures are used correctly as an upper bound ('may have'), but the placebo and nocebo literature (two reviews, neuroimaging findings) is cited without appraisal, and the cited active-placebo example in MDMA rests on a pooled phase 2 analysis that was later retracted.

domains.domain: Reliance on the authors' own studies
domains.note: One of 10 references is by the first author (a review of differential placebo effects in brain stimulation).

The unequal distribution of placebo effects and the possible nocebo effects in the placebo arm are reasoned from design and general research, with no trial data; the letter signals this with 'may' and 'likely', but its summary sentences state the boon of placebo effects as fact.

domains.domain: Balance of the argument on blinding in MAPP1 (what the trial did to protect its outcome assessment, and what its placebo arm's improvement implies, are under-represented)
domains.note: The letter does not mention the blinded independent raters or the improvement of about 13 points in the placebo arm (12.6 in the model, 13.9 among completers, per the trial report), and it concedes but does not weigh the clinical improvement on MDMA; it does discuss the limits of the alternatives fairly.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: No validated instrument applies to a commentary (METHODS §5.3); the editors' narrative-review checklist is used, and the overall judgment follows the worst domain (no search). The letter is a clear statement of the blinding argument and can be cited for that argument, for its derivation that up to 81 of 90 MAPP1 participants could have guessed their allocation (an upper bound), and for its call to measure blinding. It cannot be cited as evidence that expectancy or nocebo effects explain MAPP1's result, since it contains no data on them.

key_findings.finding: The authors concede that MDMA participants improved markedly in MAPP1, both groups having had psychotherapy, and say the question is how they improved.

MAPP1's placebo group received an inert pill, which the authors call insufficient for blinding; blinding was not formally measured, but from the trial's figures they calculate that 81 of 90 participants (90%) may have correctly guessed their treatment at the end of the intervention; the trial's authors defended the design, reportedly agreed with the FDA.
key_findings.note: Editors' check: MAPP1 reports at least 7 of 44 on placebo and at least 2 of 46 on MDMA believing they were in the other group (at least 9 of 90), so 81 of 90 is the maximum possible number of correct guesses, not an observed count.

key_findings.finding: The main concern is an unequal distribution of placebo effects: psychedelics have immediate, recognisable effects, so participants will likely know whether they are on the drug; citing reviews, the authors say placebo effects can change activity in the amygdala and stress-response circuits and the release of serotonin, dopamine and endogenous opioids, and that highly publicised treatments may produce large placebo effects through high expectations.
key_findings.locator: 4th paragraph (left column, continued in the right column)

key_findings.finding: Participants on MDMA received both the drug's pharmacological effects and the placebo effects of knowing they had it, whereas in an adequately blinded trial each participant's expectation would be a coin flip (50%); placebo participants lost their placebo effects, because only a small minority believed they had MDMA, and may have had nocebo effects from knowing they had missed the intervention.

Alternatives to an inert control are active placebos (a drug mimicking the acute effects, such as midazolam in ketamine trials, or a low or very low dose of the same drug, such as low-dose MDMA in some phase 2 MDMA trials, citing the 2019 pooled phase 2 analysis) and active comparators (escitalopram in a psilocybin trial); these have their own limitations, may muddle interpretation, may make a difference harder to show and may still fail to blind.
key_findings.locator: 6th paragraph (p. 1687, right column, continued on p. 1688, left column); reference 6

key_findings.finding: Trial investigators should at a minimum be required to collect data on whether blinding succeeded; the 2010 CONSORT update removed the requirement to measure blinding, leaving limited data on blinding and its effects.

The authors accept in principle the rebuttal that drug and placebo effects may both be legitimate, and may interact with psychedelic mechanisms, but say adopting it would mean judging treatments by absolute rather than placebo-relative benefit, an overhaul of how efficacy is measured in psychiatry.
key_findings.locator: 2nd paragraph (left column, ending at the top of the right column)

key_findings.finding: The authors declare no competing interests; the content is their opinion, not the official view of their institutions.

reporting_issues.issue: The 81 of 90 (90%) correct guesses are derived from MAPP1's statement that at least 9 participants believed they were in the other group, counts the trial's authors call anecdotal; the letter's 'may have' is correct, but the figure is easily read as a measured blinding result.
reporting_issues.consequence: Cite it as the most that could have guessed correctly, not as MAPP1's blinding result; MAPP2's survey (94% and 75%) is the only measured figure.

reporting_issues.issue: Reference 2 (Colloca & Barsky, 2020) ends with a stray '6.' after the year.

verification.source_read: PDF pp. 1687–1688 and the unnumbered third page (PDFs/MDMA/Burke_2021_CautionPsychedelicFrontier.pdf), all pages, read from the text layer (pdftotext -layout) and checked on pages rendered at 110 dpi for the column and paragraph layout.
